newsitem.title: USA: Deep Blue team aims to level re-match vs. Kasparov.
newsitem.headline: Deep Blue team aims to level re-match vs. Kasparov.

text.p: The team of scientists backing up the IBM supercomputer Deep Blue hope the machine can immediately level their re-match against world chess champion Garry Kasparov in Sunday's second game.

The 34-year-old Russian grandmaster won the first game of the $1.1 million contest with finesse on Saturday when he had the white pieces, sacrificing a rook for a less valuable bishop and pawn at the crucial moment in the game.
Deep Blue, the strongest chess-playing computer ever built, will have the advantage of the white pieces and the first move on Sunday. The advantage is similar to holding serve in tennis.
"Last year we won the first game we played with white and then Garry won his first game with white so I hope history will repeat itself," Deep Blue team manager Chung-Jen "CJ" Tan said.
Sunday's game starts at 3 p.m. EDT (1900 GMT). Each game can last several hours. The winner of the six-game match will collect $700,000 and the loser $400,000. The match ends on May 11.
In their contest in Philadelphia in February 1996, the computer won the first game, but Kasparov recovered with three wins and two draws in the remaining games to win the match.

The contest is part chess match and part research project to help build computers that can make complex, simultaneous calculations at high speeds. Among the applications for the technology developed for Deep Blue are weather forecasting, air traffic control, data mining and molecular dynamics.

Chess playing is considered ideal for computers because the game involves a specific number of physical objects governed by simple, clearly defined rules. Information on the contest is carried on the IBM Web site www.chess.ibm.com.

Kasparov, considered by most experts to be the best player in the history of chess, has no advance information of Deep Blue's most recent games or improvements made to its programme. Deep Blue, an IBM RS/6000 SP parallel processor with specialised microchips for chess, calculates hundreds of millions of moves per second.
IBM computer scientists have also infused Deep Blue with more knowledge of chess with the help of full-time grandmaster consultant Joel Benjamin, a former U.S. champion.

Kasparov played with authority Saturday, starting with a quiet, careful opening, then exploding in the middlegame with the sacrifice exchange of pieces that put him in charge for a winning endgame. Deep Blue resigned after 45 moves and 3 hours and 45 minutes play.
"It was a different kind of chess from how we would see Garry Kasparov playing against a human opponent," Kasparov told 450 spectators who watched Saturday's game in a Manhattan office complex.

During games, one of Deep Blue's human operators sits opposite Kasparov at a wooden chess board, a black video display screen and keyboard at his side. The operator types in all the moves on the keyboard and plays Deep Blue's move on the board.

The system resides at the IBM research centre in Yorktown Heights, New York, but a replica of the computer -- two six-foot, five-inch in tall modules containing 16 processors each -- has been installed at the match site.
